messages.author: 731f9c698c3638fc
messages.subject: Significance Tests
parts:
Hi,

I am currently trying to find the differences in vocabulary between
female and male speakers in a corpus of spoken portuguese. Rayson,
Leech and Hodges did such a test ("Social Differentation in the Use of
English Vocabular", 1997) for english based on the BNC, so my first
approach was to apply a chi sqare test for every type to see whether
the difference between the male and the female part of the corpus is
significant. I also computed the phi value to get a measurement of
distance, as described in the book "Quantitative corpus linguistics
with R".

Then I read Kilgarriff 2001 ("Comparing corpora"), who strongly
advised not to use a chi square test, but a Mann-Whitney test. So I
divided my corpus in 14 part (5 male, 9 female), randomly selected
from smaller chunks of the corpus. I then counted the number of tokens
of each type in the parts. As this is my first attempt to use a corpus
to analyze linguistic data, I just wanted to know if I used the
correct R functions with the correct parameters, especially for the
Mann-Whitney test.

For the chi square I just computed the number of tokens (here the type
is "um" = engl. "one/a"):
tokens masc = 789
tokens fem = 1159
rest of tokens masc = 70552
rest of tokens fem = 123686

In R:
> m<-matrix(c(789, 1159, 70552, 123686), byrow=T, ncol=2)
> chisq.test(m, correct=F)

Pearson's Chi-squared test

data: m
X-squared = 14.5668, df = 1, p-value = 0.0001353


Which I interpret in favor of my alternative hypothesis, that the
appearance of "um" in my corpus is not independant of gender and more
often articulated by man. The correlation is very weak (chi
square=14,57, df=1, p < 0.001, phi=0,0086).

For the Mann-Whitney Test I counted the appearance of "um" in each
part:
masc parts: 159, 155, 152, 139, 168
fem parts: 145, 132, 116, 131, 110, 141, 129, 117, 131

In R:
> count.masc = c(159, 155, 152, 139, 168)
> count.fem = c(145, 132, 116, 131, 110, 141, 129, 117, 131)
> # is masc greater than fem?
> wilcox.test(count.masc, count.fem, alternative = "g")

Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data: count.masc and count.fem
W = 43, p-value = 0.003797
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is greater than 0

> # is fem greater than masc?
> wilcox.test(count.fem, count.masc, alternative = "g")

Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data: count.masc and count.fem
W = 43, p-value = 0.9975
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is greater than 0


Which, I think, also tells me that my alternative hypothesis is true.

My first quiestion is now: Did I use the tests right here? With the
correct parameters?

I also have a more general question (maybe OT): I think I understand
the reasons why I should prefer the Mann-Whitney test here: because it
does not prefer tokens with high frequency and because a greater
corpus means more significant difference between two of its parts in a
chi square test (even if I would divide it randomly)...? But is the
Mann-Whitney test the best thing I can do here? Given my question
(difference for each type between the male and female part, with
distance measurement), what other tests are there that may be used
here?

Peter

messages.author: 530a6629d0d55cb6
messages.subject: RE: [CorpLing with R] Significance Tests
parts:
Hi Peter,

I can't comment on the R code (yet) but can offer some thoughts on
Chi-squared and Mann-Whitney. Following the 1997 paper, I worked on a
comparison of X2 with G2 i.e. chi-squared and log-likelihood (LL, or
likelihood ratio). If you take a look at:

http://ucrel.lancs.ac.uk/llwizard.html

then you can see further information about LL and more papers. The
comparison paper was published at JADT 2004 and shows the limits of
reliability of X2 and G2 for the corpus comparison scenario e.g.
keywords. I think the Mann-Whitney test has some drawbacks and I mention
this in my PhD and in a recent IJES paper:

"Due to problems of too many zeros in the Mann-Whitney test, Kilgarriff
(2001) reported that his technique omits words with less than 30
occurrences in the joint LOB and Brown corpus. This is a major drawback
with the Mann-Whitney test; here it omits 92% of the types in the joint
corpus. [....] These points suggest that the Mann-Whitney ranks test is
suitable only for investigating mid- to high-frequency words when
comparing corpora of the same size".

Other papers have used Fishers Exact test as an alternative to X2 and
G2, but that was in the area of assessing collocation strength where the
frequencies tend to be even more skewed than with keyness comparisons.

Hope that helps.

Regards,
Paul.

Computing Department, Infolab21, Lancaster University, Lancaster, LA1
4WA, UK.

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Significance Tests
parts: Hi
> Then I read Kilgarriff 2001 ("Comparing corpora"), who strongly advised not to use a chi square test, but a Mann-Whitney test.

I am of course aware of that publication but I must say that I find
Adam's warnings against the Chi-square test are to some degree
exaggerated. One of admittedly several reasons against the chi-square
test (and other significance tests) he discusses is that significance
tests test produce too many significant results given the large n in
corpus studies. However, on the basis of a simulation in which I make
45 pairwise comparisons of corpus parts I could show that this problem
can completely disappear once required correction for multipe post hoc
tests is applied: while regular chi-square tests yielded more than
20.45% significant results (i.e., more than 4 times as many than
expected by chance), the post hoc correction was quite (positively)
conservative, resulting in only 3.7% (95% CI: 0.5%). Thus, this reason
at least does not really apply; as I say in that paper: "While these
results do of course not contradict the general methodological point
that with a large enough sample we will get a significant result, the
results do contradict Kilgarriff’s statement that “arbitrary
associations between word frequencies and corpora are systematically
non-random”: Once the prescriptively correct statistical procedure is
adopted, we get the desired result that the random baseline of false
hits is not exceeded even with chi-square tests on word frequencies".

Now, as for your way of using the Mann-Whitney test. I don't have
Adam's paper here, but I at least would use a different approach
because your approach appears to be dependent on the corpus parts'
sizes. If the female data made up only 10% of the corpus, then of
course the Mann-Whitney test would return a significant result even of
the proportion of a word would reflect that perfectly:

female.data<-c(36, 65, 63,12, 56)
male.data<-c(325, 584, 568, 107, 505) # nearly exactly 9 times as many
wilcox.test(female.data, male.data) # p<0.05 although this reflects
only the corpus size

So, it would be better to run the Mann-Whitney test on the relative
frequencies of occurrence.

female.corpus.size<-111111
male.corpus.size<-1000000
female.data<-c(36, 65, 63,12, 56)/female.corpus.size
male.data<-c(325, 584, 568, 107, 505)/male.corpus.size
wilcox.test(female.data, male.data) # p=1, now as expected

(Note that this does not take of Stefan Evert's point of independence
of data points etc., the handling of which would require you, as one
alternative at least, to compute a speaker-specific (!) ratio of word
uses and compare those with wilcox.test.)

Just my $0.02,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

University of California, Santa Barbara

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Re: Significance Tests
parts: Hi

> thank you very much for your suggestions. I will use the correction in my Mann-Whitney test and will also try to use log likelihood as another test. Is there any R function that I could use here (calculating the G2 an p value at once)?

I don't know of any convenient R function for that. There is a kinda
backwards way to get that from a Poisson regression but you don't want
to do that, it's cumbersome. You can compute it semi-manually tho. If
you define obs and exp like this

obs<-matrix(c(10, 20, 30, 40), ncol=2)
exp<-chisq.test(obs, correct=F)$exp

and then apply the logic from <http://ucrel.lancs.ac.uk/llwizard.html> ...
> Do you think that the Fisher's exact test would also be an alternative?

Yes, and I would log10 the p-value.

Just to make that clear: in spite of their frequency of use, both
log-likelihood and Fisher-Yates exact don't account for Evert's issue
(but hardly anyone does yet).
> And, Stefan, what would be the paper you wrote about the correction for post hoc tests?

<http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/research/overview-research.html>,
then the paper/download at 2005b.

Cheers,

STG
--

Hi,

I did some experiments with the statistical tests you mentioned, and I
am now confused on a higher level:

1) The Mann-Whitney-Test for relative frequencies does not seem to be
suitable; I calculated all values as proposed (division by male/female
corpus size), now only very frequent types are ranked high in "more
often uttered by male than by female speakers", while only types with
very low frequency are ranked high in the "female" table. I think this
is not what would be expected...

2) I compared the log likelihood values to the chi square values,
which only gave minor differences. Most of the differences concern
words with a frequency of zero (or very low) on either the male or the
female side of the corpus, which rank higher when using the ll test...
Is this expected? This also leads directly to my next problem:

3) I read through Evert's papers and now I want to do a dispersion
test for my types. Stefan, I think that this is what you meant when
you proposed the wilcox.test "to compute a speaker-specific (!) ratio
of word", right? How would I apply the wilcox.test here? Evert,
following Bayeen, proposes a Monte Carlo simulation; is there an R
function for that (I looked through his UCS/R package but couldn't
find the right test...)? What other tests would you propose to test
whether my types are underdispersed within my corpus?

Peter

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Re: Significance Tests
parts:
Hi

[sorry for delay, just teaching my bootcamp, which keeps me busy ...]

Well, the log-likelihood test is particularly good at handling lower
frequencies (compared to chi-square so it's not a surprise that this
is where most differences show up. As for the dispersion measure, I
was thinking of (i) avoiding chi-square tests on overall freqs because
the data violate the independence assumption and (ii) using a test
that is capable of handling dependent samples, but I am not in a
position to make concrete suggestions for data I know very little
about. I can, however, (i) tell you that off the top of my head I know
of no ready-made function for such a Monte-Carlo sampling approach,
and (ii) suggest where you can find something on measures of
dispersion, namely in a recent IJCL article that surveys, AFAIK, all
existing dispersion measures:
<http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/research/Dispe...@IJCL.pdf>.
(In a follow-up study, Juilland's D for unequal corpus parts and DP
give the best results.

HTH,

STG
--

thank you very much for your suggestions, it was a pleasure for me to
read through your article. It really helped a lot to learn about all
the dispersion tests at once in comparison, I think I will use the two
tests you favoured: Juilland's D and DP. Your R functions for the
dispersion tests work like a charm.

Now I have only one other question, which may sound kind of stupid to
an expert: You mentioned that "the data violates the independence
assumption". Why is that? When I prepared the data and thought about
the tests, I assumed that my two variables "gender" and "word usage"
would be independent. Or did I miss something here?

Peter

speaker/writer contributes more than one data point; cf.

good overview.
